messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Our university team is entering a contest. Target apogee is around 375 m. Motor no bigger than 24 mm. It needs to come down at 6 m/s or less. It should handle 4 m/s wind. Please flag anything risky.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 375 m (approximate, within 5%, so roughly 356 to 394 m). Motor diameter at most 24 mm (maximum). Landing at most 6 m/s (maximum). Wind is 4 m/s (fixed). Rail length, launch angle and site altitude are not given, so I assume a 1.5 m rail, a vertical launch and sea level. Single stage.
2. Feasibility: no-drag burnout speed for 375 m is sqrt(2*9.81*375) = 86 m/s. A 24 mm or 18 mm sport rocket gives a lot of that back to drag, so a C or a small D is the likely class, and anything 29 mm is illegal under the motor-diameter cap. I need the case diameters and impulses before I pick one.

2. Feasibility: C6 and C11 are both 8.8 N*s. The C6 is an 18 mm case (0.018 m by 0.07 m, 0.0231 kg, 4.8 N average) and the C11 is 24 mm (0.024 m, 11.3 N average, 0.0353 kg). The D12 is also 24 mm but 16.8 N*s, which on a light rocket would sail well past 375 m. The E12 is 27.1 N*s and still 24 mm, so it is legal on diameter and far too much impulse. A C6 in a slim cardboard tube is the closest match. All four motors are at or under 24 mm.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.040 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 4.8 / (0.040 * 9.81) = 12.2. Pad weight is 0.040 * 9.81 = 0.392 N, so rail acceleration is (4.8 - 0.392) / 0.040 = 110 m/s^2 and exit speed is sqrt(2 * 110 * 1.5) = 18.2 m/s. That clears 15 m/s on the average thrust, and the C6 spike should add more. Propellant is 0.011 kg, descent mass 0.040 - 0.011 = 0.029 kg. A 5 m/s chute at Cd 0.8 needs 2 * 0.029 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.0232 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.0232 / 3.1416) = 0.17 m. I will fly a 0.30 m chute so the landing stays under 6 m/s if the rocket is heavier than this guess. Burn is 1.83 s; a 5 s delay ejects near 7 s, about when a flight this size reaches apogee.
4. Draft: 0.09 m ogive polystyrene nose on a 0.32 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.022 m, wall 0.4 mm. Motor mount 0.019 m outside, 0.07 m long, cardboard, Estes C6 with a 5 s delay. Three balsa fins, root 0.050 m, tip 0.020 m, span 0.035 m, sweep 0.022 m, 1.6 mm thick. Chute 0.30 m polyethylene, Cd 0.8, on ejection. Wind for the flight is 4 m/s; the rail stays the default 1.5 m.

4. Check: the simulator gives 407.6 m. The band for about 375 m is 5%, and (407.6 - 375) / 375 = 8.7%, so 407.6 - 375 = 32.6 m too high. The rest passes: rail exit 29.7 m/s, thrust-to-weight 12.2, margin 1.22 cal at the rail and through the burn, landing 2.9 m/s. Mass is 0.0401 kg, which matches the guess. The chute opens at 6.9 s, just before the 7.13 s apogee. Drift is 534 m in the 4 m/s wind, which is a long walk but not a stated limit.
5. Fix: apogee 407.6 m is the miss. The motor is already the small one, so I am adding mass rather than stepping up to a D. A 0.005 kg clay nose weight is 0.005 / 0.0401 = 12% of the liftoff mass, placed at the top of the tube. That also moves the CG forward, so the 1.22 cal margin should rise, not fall.

4. Check: 5 g of clay barely moved the altitude. The simulator gives 403.9 m, and (403.9 - 375) / 375 = 7.7%, still outside the 5% band. 403.9 - 375 = 28.9 m high. Gates all pass: rail exit 28.0 m/s, thrust-to-weight 10.8, margin 2.17 cal, landing 3.1 m/s. The weight did what I expected for stability and almost nothing for altitude: 407.6 m fell only to 403.9 m.
5. Fix: the failing value is 403.9 m. Nose mass is the wrong lever on this rocket, and the margin is 2.17 cal, so there is room to add fin area. I am enlarging the balsa fins only: root 0.050 m to 0.065 m, tip 0.020 m to 0.028 m, span 0.035 m to 0.050 m, sweep 0.022 m to 0.030 m. The extra fin drag should pull the apogee down toward 375 m. The 5 g weight stays.

4. Check: the larger fins did the job. The simulator gives 369.3 m, and 375 - 369.3 = 5.7 m, which is 5.7 / 375 = 1.5% low, inside the 5% band. Rail exit 27.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 10.6, margin 2.8 cal at the rail and through the burn, landing 3.2 m/s. The C6 is an 18 mm motor, under the 24 mm cap. Chute opens at 6.9 s, just before the 7.12 s apogee. Drift is 431 m at 4 m/s of wind. That is the risk worth flagging: a 2.8 cal margin will weathercock, and the walk back is long. Nothing in the request caps the drift, and the landing speed is fine.
5. Fix: no further change. The altitude, the motor diameter and the safety gates all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 369.3 m sits near the low side of the band. If the real rocket is lighter than 0.046 kg, or the fins are sanded smaller than drawn, it climbs back toward the first draft's 400 m and can leave the band. The 4 m/s wind plus 2.8 cal of margin means the flight will not be as vertical as this zero-angle run implies, so the field needs to be big. Chute Cd is a model value; a lazy 0.30 m chute can land faster than 3.2 m/s and still be under 6.
messages.content:
C6-5 on a 22 mm cardboard tube with 5 g of nose clay and enlarged balsa fins, aimed at about 375 m.
In a 4 m/s wind the flight reaches 369 m, leaves a 1.5 m rail at 27 m/s, and lands at 3.2 m/s under a 0.30 m chute. The 18 mm motor is inside the 24 mm cap.
Risk: drift is 431 m and the 2.8 cal margin will weathercock. Give it a large field.
